title: When Similarity Is Interaction-Driven: Quantum Kernels for Regime-Sensitive Learning
authors: Hanqiu Peng, Jianlong Lu, Ying Chen
abstract: Similarity in many decision systems is governed not by distance alone but by interactions among variables. In fraud and anomaly detection, small local perturbations can cross interaction-sensitive decision boundaries while leaving ambient distance almost unchanged. Motivated by this setting, we introduce a thin-slab interaction model and an interaction-driven quantum kernel constructed from entangled Pauli-string feature maps. The feature map explicitly encodes sparse high-order block interactions. We show that the resulting fidelity kernel is positive semidefinite, admits an exact block-factorized formulation, and induces a geometry sensitive to changes in interaction regime. Across balanced and imbalanced synthetic experiments spanning third-, fourth-, sixth-, and eighth-order interactions, the proposed kernel consistently outperforms linear, radial basis function, Laplacian, and polynomial kernels, as well as an engineered-interaction linear baseline supplied with the planted block products. On real fraud-detection benchmarks, it achieves the highest mean accuracy and F1 on Credit Card Fraud Detection and ranks second on IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection. These findings show that quantum-kernel performance depends on alignment between feature-map geometry and the underlying predictive structure, rather than on Hilbert-space dimension alone. Because the prescribed block-factorized kernel can also be evaluated exactly on a classical computer, the results establish predictive and representational value rather than computational quantum speedup.
summary: This work proposes an interaction-driven quantum kernel designed for machine learning tasks where data similarity depends on complex, high-order variable interactions. By encoding these interactions via entangled Pauli-string feature maps, the kernel achieves superior predictive performance on synthetic and real-world fraud detection benchmarks. The study emphasizes that the advantage lies in the feature-map's geometric alignment with the underlying physical structure, rather than quantum computational speedup.
main_problem: The paper addresses how similarity in complex decision systems, such as fraud detection, is governed by high-order interactions between variables rather than simple Euclidean distance.
main_result: The proposed interaction-driven quantum kernel consistently outperforms standard kernels on synthetic benchmarks and achieves state-of-the-art performance on real-world fraud detection datasets.
method: They introduce a thin-slab interaction model and construct a quantum kernel using entangled Pauli-string feature maps that explicitly encode sparse, high-order block interactions.
model_or_system: The model is a quantum kernel applied to data structured into disjoint blocks, where the label generation is based on planted high-order block interactions, creating a regime-sensitive learning task.
key_observables: Mean accuracy and F1 score on fraud detection benchmarks; the kernel's ability to induce a geometry sensitive to interaction regimes.
important_parameters: Interaction order (up to eighth-order); input dimension (up to 80 dimensions); imbalance ratio of the data.
main_assumptions: The performance advantage is shown to be predictive and representational, not necessarily evidence of a computational quantum speedup, as the kernel is classically evaluable.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the thin-slab model, proposes the interaction-driven quantum kernel, proves its theoretical properties (PSD, block-factorized), and validates its performance through controlled synthetic experiments across various interaction orders, culminating in real-world fraud detection benchmarks.
why_interesting: While the application is in ML, the use of entangled Pauli-string feature maps and the focus on encoding specific, high-order correlations relates to how complex quantum states can represent structured correlations, which is relevant to understanding entanglement structure in many-body systems.
